task_brief: Day 2 of "Critical Response, Aesthetics, and Historical Context" (unit 5, grade 9) is a first concept model on critique protocols and evidence-based feedback. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Write a sustained evidence-based critical response comparing two works across historical and cultural context. Today's work contributes to that by handling critique protocols and evidence-based feedback at the concept model a stage, against the unit's wider topics of describe analyse interpret and evaluate, critique protocols and evidence-based feedback, movements and historical context, and cultural context and respectful interpretation. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Study the first model work for critique protocols and evidence-based feedback closely before making anything of your own. Write what you notice in three passes: first what is literally there, then how it is put together, then what effect that has on a viewer or listener. Name the specific choice the maker used to create critique protocols and evidence-based feedback. Then reproduce that one element — not the whole work — in your own short study, and write one sentence on what was harder than it looked. Use only public-domain, openly licensed, or supplied model works, and cite whatever you studied. Use the attached Academy-original Model A as the first model work; no outside search or teacher-supplied example is required. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about critique protocols and evidence-based feedback, and it belongs to "Critical Response, Aesthetics, and Historical Context", which also covers separate topics such as describe analyse interpret and evaluate. Close out with this check before you stop: Explain the modelled approach to critique protocols and evidence-based feedback in your own words and name the step most likely to go wrong. At grade 9 the bar is independent work with explicit criteria set before you start, and evidence that you evaluated the finished result against those criteria rather than against how it felt.

sourceReference:
ATTACHED MANUEL ACADEMY LEARNER RESOURCE

Resource ID: ma-resource:ma-g9-arts-and-music-u05-l02

Lesson focus: critique protocols and evidence-based feedback

Resource type: ACADEMY_ORIGINAL_MODEL

MODEL A — "Meeting Place," a described paper construction of overlapping door-shaped forms made from imaginary transit tickets. Blue forms cluster at the edges; one orange form is central. A caption says the maker considered how shared spaces can welcome some people while confusing others. Separate observation, supplied context, and an interpretation supported by a visible choice. Use it to study critique protocols and evidence-based feedback; describe evidence before judging and adapt the example rather than copying a finished work.

How to use it: Use the attached Academy-original Model A as the first model work; no outside search or teacher-supplied example is required.

Rights: Manuel Academy original; licensed CC BY 4.0 for learner use and adaptation. No third-party text, image, score, lyric, melody, recording, or performance is included.

Access and materials: Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.
critique_criteria: Observation is recorded in three distinct passes: literal content, construction, and effect.
The specific maker's choice that creates critique protocols and evidence-based feedback is named, not described in general praise.
One element — not the whole work — is reproduced as a short study, with a note on what proved harder than expected.
Every studied work is public domain, openly licensed, or supplied for this task, and is cited.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.

Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, notated, constructed, or demonstrated responses. Where performance is the target, a private demonstration to one trusted adult carries the same weight as any audience, and requires no recording.
Provide adaptive instruments and grips, enlarged or braille notation, seated and standing studio access, low-odour and low-dust material substitutes, and hearing protection on request.

Where documentation quality is itself the target, document the artwork alone with no person in frame, or have an adult verify the physical work directly. Neither route requires an image of the learner, and both preserve the documentation target rather than replacing it.
task_accessibility_provisions: Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Public performance is never required. A private, low-audience, or written-and-scored alternative always carries the same academic target.
No recording of the learner’s voice, no photograph, and no video is ever required; documentation may be written, notated, sketched, or adult-verified instead.
Use only original, public-domain, licensed, or family-approved works. Do not reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or other protected works without documented rights.
The tutor may explain technique, ask diagnostic questions, and critique work, but never silently completes graded creative work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting critique protocols and evidence-based feedback.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for critique protocols and evidence-based feedback follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for critique protocols and evidence-based feedback, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to critique protocols and evidence-based feedback works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of critique protocols and evidence-based feedback, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking critique protocols and evidence-based feedback mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply critique protocols and evidence-based feedback under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on critique protocols and evidence-based feedback rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
